parole.significato: One affected with.
parole.testo: From French -acque, from New Latin -acus, from Ancient Greek -ακός (-akós, “-ic”). Related to -ic and -y.

parole.significato: The act of making acetous or sour; the process of converting, or of becoming converted, into vinegar.
parole.testo: Circa 1733. Directly or via French acétification, from New Latin acētificātiō, from acētum (“vinegar”) + -ficātiō, from faciō (“to make”).

parole.significato: A small, dry, indehiscent fruit, containing a single seed, as in the buttercup.
parole.testo: From French achène and its source, New Latin achena, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “a-”) + χαίνω (khaínō, “to gape”).

parole.significato: A chronic disease marked by enlargement of the bones of the extremities, face, and jaw that is caused by over-activity…
parole.testo: From French acromégalie, from New Latin acromegalia, from Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “tip, extremity”) and μέγας (mégas, “large”). By surface analysis, acro- + -megaly.

parole.significato: Of or relating to lymphatic glands or lymphoid tissue.
parole.testo: Late 19th century borrowing from French adénoïde, from New Latin adenoīdēs, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓δενοειδής (ădenoeidḗs, “glandular”), from ᾰ̓δήν (ădḗn, “gland”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-oid, -like”); equivalent to aden- + -oid. The noun is derived from ellipsis of tumeur adénoïde (“glandular

parole.significato: The design, construction, mathematics, and mechanics of aircraft and other flying objects; the study of and control of…
parole.testo: From French aéronautique or New Latin aeronauticus. Equivalent to aero- + -naut + -ics.

parole.significato: The gases surrounding the Earth or any astronomical body.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French atmosphère, from New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “steam”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”); corresponding to atmo- + -sphere.

parole.significato: Either of the two main arteries that supply blood to the head of which the left in humans arises from the arch of the a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French carotide or New Latin carōtides, from Ancient Greek κᾰρωτῐ́δες (kărōtĭ́des, “carotid arteries”), from κᾰρόω (kăróō, “to plunge into deep sleep or torpor”) + -τῐ́δες (-tĭ́des, plural nominal suffix), from the fact that the carotid artery supplies blood to the brain, and interrupt

parole.significato: A constituent part of a flower pistil: the female reproductive organs in a flower. A carpel is composed of an ovary, a…
parole.testo: 1835, borrowed from French carpelle, from New Latin carpellum, a diminutive of Ancient Greek κᾰρπός (kărpós, “fruit”), from Proto-Indo-European *kerp- (“to pluck, harvest”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the neck.
parole.testo: Borrowing from French cervical, from New Latin cervīcālis, from cervīx (“the neck, nape”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, cervic- + -al.

parole.significato: A widely distributed edible mushroom, Cantharellus cibarius, being yellow and trumpet-shaped; or any similar mushroom o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chanterelle, from New Latin cantharellus, diminutive of Latin cantharus (“drinking vessel”), from Ancient Greek κάνθαρος (kántharos). Probably of Pre-Greek origin, cognate with Akkadian 𒃶𒁺𒊒𒌑 (/⁠kanduru⁠/, “kind of vessel”), from Sumerian 𒄑𒃶𒉡𒌉 (/⁠gannu-tur⁠/, “small vessel; potst

parole.significato: That produces colored precipitates
parole.testo: From French colorifique or New Latin colorificus, from color + -i- + -ficus.

parole.significato: One of the corneas of a compound eye in certain invertebrates.
parole.testo: From French cornéule, from New Latin corneola, diminutive of cornea. By surface analysis, cornea + ule.

parole.significato: The art of criticism.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French critique, from New Latin critica (“critique”), feminine of criticus (“critical”); see critic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to deism and deists.
parole.testo: From French déiste, from New Latin deista, from Latin Deus (“God”) + -ista (“-ist”).

parole.significato: To demarcate.
parole.testo: From French démarquer, from New Latin *demarcō (“to mark off, set the bounds of, bound”), from Latin dē- (“off”) + Medieval Latin marcō (“to mark”), from marca (“bound, mark, march”). By surface analysis, de- + mark. See mark, march.

parole.significato: Concerning the relationships between the governments of countries.
parole.testo: From French diplomatique and its etymon New Latin diplōmaticus. By surface analysis, diplomat + -ic.

parole.significato: A petty pedant, a person who complains about minor mistakes.
parole.testo: A modification of doriphore, borrowed from French doryphore (“Colorado beetle”) by Harold Nicolson in 1952, presumably under the influence of the various senses of pest. The French term was a translation of the New Latin genus Doryphora, itself from Ancient Greek δορυφόρος (doruphóros, “lance-bearin

parole.significato: The tendency to think selfishly with exclusive self-interest in mind.
parole.testo: From French égoïsme, from New Latin egoismus, from Latin ego. By surface analysis, ego + -ism.

parole.significato: Capable of stretching; particularly, capable of stretching so as to return to an original shape or size when force is r…
parole.testo: From French élastique, from New Latin elasticus (“elastic”), from Ancient Greek ἐλαστός (elastós), alternative form of ἐλατός (elatós, “ductile”) (cf. ἐλατήρ (elatḗr, “a driver, hurler”)), from ἐλαύνω (elaúnō, “to drive, set in motion, push, strike, beat out”).

parole.significato: A stable suspension of small droplets of one liquid in another with which it is immiscible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French émulsion, from New Latin ēmulsiō, ēmulsiōnis, based on Latin ēmulgeō (“to milk out, extract”).

parole.significato: A discrete but connected event, situation, or period within a broader sequence, narrative, or life course.
parole.testo: From French épisode, from New Latin *epīsodium, from Ancient Greek ἐπεισόδιον (epeisódion, “a parenthetic addition, episode”), neuter of ἐπεισόδιος (epeisódios, “following upon the entrance, coming in besides, adventitious”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + εἰς (eis, “into”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way”).

parole.significato: Related to Europe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French européen, itself from New Latin Eurōpaeānus, from the secondary stem Eurōpae- extracted from the Classical Latin adjective Eurōpaeus [from Ancient Greek Εὐρωπαῖος (Eurōpaîos, “European”), from Εὐρώπᾱ (Eurṓpā, “Europe”) + -ῐος (-ĭos, suffix forming adjectives)] + -ānus (“-an”). B

parole.significato: A French antiship missile.
parole.testo: From French Exocet, from exocet (“flying fish”), from New Latin exocoetus, from Ancient Greek ἐξώκοιτος (exṓkoitos, “a kind of fish resting on shore”), from ἔξω (éxō, “out, outside, without”) + κοῖτος (koîtos, “place of rest, bed”).

parole.significato: Any member of a class of molluscs (Gastropoda) that includes snails, slugs, and limpets; univalve mollusc.
parole.testo: From French gastéropode, from gastro- + -poda, New Latin, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr, “stomach”) and πούς (poús, “foot”).

parole.significato: An elemental (spirit or corporeal creature associated with a classical element) associated with earth.
parole.testo: From French gnome (“gnome”), from New Latin gnomus, used by Paracelsus as a synonym for pygmaeus (“pygmy”).

parole.significato: Shaped like the Greek letter lambda
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lambdoïde, from the New Latin lambdoīdēs, from the Ancient Greek λαβδοειδής (labdoeidḗs).

parole.significato: Sexual stimulation of one's genitalia or other erotic regions, often to the point of orgasm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French masturbation, New Latin masturbātiō, masturbātiōnem. By surface analysis, masturbat(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the metric system of measurement.
parole.testo: From French métrique (1864), from New Latin metricus (“pertaining to the system based on the meter”), from metrum (“a meter”); see meter. By surface analysis, metre + -ic.

parole.significato: The smallest particle of a specific element or compound that retains the chemical properties of that element or compoun…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French molécule, from New Latin molecula (“a molecule”), diminutive of Latin moles (“a mass”).

parole.significato: A soft-bodied invertebrate of the phylum Mollusca, typically with a hard shell of one or more pieces.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mollusque, from New Latin Mollusca (phylum name), from Latin molluscus (“thin-shelled”), from mollis (“soft”).

parole.significato: The organic compound 3,5-dihydroxytoluene, found in many lichens and synthesizable from toluene.
parole.testo: From French orcine, from New Latin orcina, from Dutch orseille, from French orseille, from Old French orchel, orseil, from Old Catalan orxella (influenced by dialectal Arabic [script needed] ('urjālla)), from Italian oricello, from Latin ōricilla, diminutive of ōricula (variant of auricula), both di

parole.significato: Of or relating to the palate or to a palatine bone.
parole.testo: Borrowing from French palatin, from New Latin palātīnus, from palātum (“the palate”) + -īnus (“-ine”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to palate + -ine.

parole.significato: Synonym of pedipalp.
parole.testo: * (verb): From French palper. * (noun): From New Latin palpus (“a feeler”). * Both ultimately from Latin palpō (“to stroke, touch softly, feel”).

parole.significato: The sterile parts of a flower; collectively, the sepals and petals (or tepals).
parole.testo: From French périanthe, from New Latin perianthium.

parole.significato: The outermost layer, or skin, of a ripe fruit or ovary.
parole.testo: From French péricarpe, from New Latin pericarpium, from Ancient Greek περικάρπιον (perikárpion, “pod, husk, shell”), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + καρπός (karpós, “fruit”). By surface analysis, peri- + -carp.

parole.significato: An organism having characteristics of both plants and animals; a zoophyte, later chiefly an animal with structural rese…
parole.testo: From plant + animal, after French plant-animal (obsolete), from New Latin plantanimal (16th c.), after Hellenistic Ancient Greek ζωόφυτον (zōóphuton, “zoophyte”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the pterygoid process of the sphenoid bone and the palatine bone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ptérygo-palatin, from New Latin pterygopalātīnus, from pterygoīdēs (“winglike”) + palātīnus (“relating to the palate”); equivalent to pterygo- + palatine.

parole.significato: An edited or censored version of a document; a product resulting from the process of editing or censoring.
parole.testo: From French rédaction or its etymon New Latin redactiō (“redaction”), from Latin redigō (“to lead back, collect, prepare, reduce to a certain state”), from red- (“back”) + agō (“to put in motion, to drive”). By surface analysis, redact + -ion.

parole.significato: One of the component parts of the calyx, particularly when such components are not fused into a single structure.
parole.testo: From French sépale, from New Latin sepalum.

parole.significato: sleepwalking
parole.testo: From French somnambulisme, from New Latin somnambulus, from Latin somnus (“sleep”) + ambulō (“to walk”), + -ism.

parole.significato: A partial dislocation of a joint, in which the articulating surfaces remain in partial contact.
parole.testo: From French subluxation, from New Latin subluxatio, from subluxare (“to subluxate, to partially displace”) + -atio (“-ation: forming abstract nouns”), from sub- (“sub-: under, below, lesser”) + luxare (“to dislocate; to displace”) after the model of Ancient Greek παράρθρημα (parárthrēma). Equivalent

parole.significato: Any salt or ester of sulfuric acid.
parole.testo: From French sulfate, from New Latin sulphatum, taken from the expression acidum sulphatum (“sulfuric acid”), from sulphatus, from Latin sulphur (“sulfur”). The term was first used in 1787 by the French chemist L. B. G. De Morveau. Equivalent to sulf(ur) + -ate (“salt or ester”).

parole.significato: Showing symptoms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French symptomatique, from New Latin symptomaticus, from Ancient Greek συμπτωματικός (sumptōmatikós, “of or pertaining to a chance (or a symptom), casual”), from σύμπτωμα (súmptōma, “a symptom”). By surface analysis, symptom + -atic.

parole.significato: Any component of the perianth (outermost whorls of flower parts, not involved in reproduction), especially when the com…
parole.testo: From French tépale, from New Latin tēpalum, coined 1827 by transposition of French pétale (“petal”).

parole.significato: A condition characterized by painful muscular spasms, caused by faulty calcium metabolism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tétanie, from New Latin tetania.

parole.significato: Pertaining to heat or temperature.
parole.testo: From French thermal, from New Latin *thermalis, from Ancient Greek θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“to heat, warm”).

parole.significato: The transversal part of a church, which crosses at right angles to the greatest length, and between the nave and choir.…
parole.testo: From French transept, from New Latin transeptum, from Latin trans- (“across”) + saeptum (“fence, partition, enclosure”).

parole.significato: A hair- or scale-like extension of the epidermis of a plant.
parole.testo: From French trichome, from New Latin trichoma, from Ancient Greek τρίχωμα (tríkhōma), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”) or independently from tricho- + -ome. Doublet of trichoma.

parole.significato: The worship of animals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French zoolâtrie, New Latin zoolatria, from zoo- + -latry.
